title: Hypertension: Confirm the Diagnosis, Then Treat Risk
bottomLine: Chronic hypertension is diagnosed with validated standardized measurement and confirmation rather than one casual office reading. Management combines cardiovascular-risk assessment, lifestyle support and pharmacotherapy matched to current Canadian thresholds, comorbidity and tolerability, while acute target-organ injury is handled on a separate emergency pathway.
recognize: Hypertension is usually asymptomatic; headache alone does not define a hypertensive emergency.
White-coat and masked hypertension make home or ambulatory measurements valuable when available.
differentiate: Severe asymptomatic blood pressure elevation is different from hypertensive emergency, which requires acute target-organ injury.
Abrupt/resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, renal disease, endocrine symptoms, sleep apnea or medication/substance exposure can suggest secondary causes.
assessment: Repeat BP with correct cuff size and standardized technique; assess orthostasis where relevant, total cardiovascular risk, CKD/diabetes/ASCVD, pregnancy potential and medication/substance contributors.
workup: Use current Canadian baseline cardiovascular/renal risk testing and out-of-office confirmation where appropriate.
Order secondary-cause testing only when history, examination or routine data justify it.
management: Use lifestyle therapy for all and start/intensify pharmacotherapy according to current Hypertension Canada risk-based thresholds and patient context.
For many patients needing medication, low-dose combination therapy is efficient; individualize for frailty, orthostasis, pregnancy and compelling indications.
medicationSafety: ACE inhibitors/ARBs are avoided in pregnancy and require creatinine/potassium follow-up after initiation or meaningful titration.
Avoid routine ACE inhibitor plus ARB combination therapy.
counselling: Teach home BP technique, adherence, sodium/alcohol/smoking/activity counselling and when symptoms require urgent care.
followUp: Reassess BP, adverse effects and relevant labs after treatment changes; use home readings and symptoms to avoid overtreatment.
examTrap: Calling one nonstandardized high office reading chronic hypertension—or treating an asymptomatic number as an emergency without target-organ injury.
oneLinePearl: Measure correctly, confirm appropriately, then treat total cardiovascular risk.

title: Coronary Artery Disease: Separate Stable Risk Management from Acute Ischemia
bottomLine: CAD care starts by deciding whether the patient is stable or potentially having an acute coronary syndrome. Stable disease requires symptom characterization, global risk reduction and appropriate noninvasive/anatomic testing when results will change management; unstable symptoms belong in an acute-care pathway.
recognize: Exertional pressure, dyspnea or reduced exercise tolerance can reflect myocardial ischemia even without classic chest pain.
Known ASCVD is secondary prevention and carries a different treatment threshold from primary prevention.
differentiate: New/rest/accelerating/prolonged symptoms are not 'stable CAD' until ACS is excluded.
GERD, musculoskeletal pain and anxiety can mimic angina, but risk/context matter.
assessment: Characterize symptom pattern, functional limitation, BP, lipids, diabetes, smoking, CKD, family history, prior revascularization and current antithrombotic/antianginal therapy.
workup: Use resting ECG and select functional/anatomic testing according to pretest probability, exercise capacity and baseline ECG; avoid testing that cannot change management.
Do not send suspected active ACS for routine outpatient stress testing.
management: Use guideline-directed lipid lowering, BP/diabetes control, smoking cessation, activity/cardiac rehabilitation and antiplatelet/antianginal therapy when indicated.
Refer for cardiology/revascularization assessment when symptoms remain limiting, high-risk anatomy/ischemia is suspected or diagnosis is uncertain.
medicationSafety: Nitrates can worsen hypotension and interact dangerously with recent PDE-5 inhibitor use.
Antiplatelet/anticoagulant combinations require explicit indication and bleeding-risk review.
counselling: Teach emergency symptoms, medication adherence, smoking cessation and graded return to activity/cardiac rehabilitation.
followUp: Track symptoms, functional status and secondary-prevention targets; revisit diagnosis if the pattern changes.
examTrap: Calling recurrent rest pain 'stable CAD' because the patient already has a coronary diagnosis.
oneLinePearl: Stable CAD is stable only when the symptom pattern is stable.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society Secondary Prevention Pathway and coronary disease resources

title: Heart Failure: Define EF Phenotype, Congestion, and Perfusion
bottomLine: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome requiring symptoms/signs plus objective cardiac evidence; ejection fraction defines treatment phenotype but does not replace volume/perfusion assessment. HFrEF and HFnrEF/HFpEF share congestion/risk management but differ in disease-modifying evidence and comorbidity priorities.
recognize: Orthopnea, PND, edema, elevated JVP, congestion and exercise intolerance support HF, while cool extremities, hypotension, oliguria or altered mentation suggest low-output instability.
Normal EF does not exclude heart failure.
differentiate: BNP/NT-proBNP supports probability but is influenced by age, renal function, AF and obesity.
COPD, anemia, obesity/deconditioning, renal disease and venous insufficiency can mimic parts of the syndrome.
assessment: Assess congestion, perfusion, BP, rhythm, ischemia, medication adherence, sodium/NSAIDs, kidney function, precipitating infection/arrhythmia and goals of care.
workup: Use ECG, renal function/electrolytes, CBC and other cause-directed tests; echocardiography defines EF/structure and natriuretic peptides can support diagnosis when uncertainty remains.
management: For HFrEF, implement the four foundational disease-modifying classes rapidly as tolerated plus diuretics for congestion.
For HFnrEF/HFpEF, use the 2025 CCS/CHFS approach emphasizing SGLT2 inhibitor therapy where appropriate, congestion control and aggressive treatment of AF, BP, obesity, CKD and other drivers.
medicationSafety: Monitor renal function, potassium and BP with RAAS/ARNI/MRA therapy; SGLT2 inhibitors require sick-day/perioperative counselling.
Do not aggressively start/titrate beta-blockade in shock or severe unstable decompensation.
redFlags: Rapid renal decline/oliguria with low perfusion
counselling: Teach daily symptom/weight awareness, sodium/medication adherence, NSAID avoidance and when to seek urgent care.
followUp: After decompensation or medication change, reassess volume status, BP, renal function/electrolytes and foundational therapy completion.
examTrap: Treating a preserved EF as evidence that heart failure is impossible—or using diuretics as a substitute for HFrEF disease-modifying therapy.
oneLinePearl: EF classifies heart failure; congestion, perfusion and comorbidity determine what you do today.

title: Atrial Fibrillation: Stroke Prevention, Rate or Rhythm, and the Patient's Goals
bottomLine: AF management has separate decisions: hemodynamic stability, stroke prevention and symptom/rhythm strategy. Do not let the rate-control versus rhythm-control question distract from anticoagulation assessment or from urgent cardioversion when instability is caused by AF.
recognize: AF produces an irregularly irregular atrial rhythm and can present with palpitations, dyspnea, fatigue, chest discomfort or no symptoms.
AF plus hypotension, ischemia, pulmonary edema or shock may require urgent synchronized cardioversion.
differentiate: Atrial flutter/other SVT and frequent ectopy can mimic AF on pulse examination; confirm rhythm on ECG.
Rate control manages ventricular response; rhythm control aims to restore/maintain sinus rhythm and is selected based on symptoms, duration, comorbidity and patient preference.
assessment: Assess stability, AF duration/onset certainty, symptoms, HF/valvular disease, thyroid/alcohol/sleep apnea triggers, stroke/bleeding risk and medication interactions.
workup: Obtain ECG and selected electrolytes/thyroid/echo or ambulatory testing based on context; evaluate thromboembolic risk before elective cardioversion/rhythm strategy.
management: Use CCS/CHRS integrated AF care including CHADS-65 based stroke-prevention logic, appropriate rate control or early rhythm-control strategy and risk-factor treatment.
Refer symptomatic recurrent AF, drug intolerance, ablation candidates or complex structural disease to rhythm specialists.
medicationSafety: AV-nodal blockers can worsen bradycardia/hypotension; non-DHP calcium-channel blockers are avoided in significant HFrEF.
Antiarrhythmics have structural-heart, QT, organ and interaction constraints and should be matched to the patient.
counselling: Explain that feeling better after rate/rhythm control does not remove stroke risk when anticoagulation is indicated.
followUp: Reassess symptoms, rate/rhythm burden, anticoagulant adherence/bleeding and modifiable drivers such as BP, alcohol, obesity and sleep apnea.
examTrap: Focusing only on heart rate while forgetting stroke prevention—or cardioverting an unstable patient only after a lengthy outpatient workup.
oneLinePearl: AF care is three questions: stable, protected from stroke, and rate or rhythm strategy.
sourceBasis: CCS/CHRS Atrial Fibrillation Guideline 2020 and current CCS resources

title: Stable Angina: Confirm the Pattern, Control Symptoms, Reduce Events
bottomLine: Stable angina is predictable ischemic discomfort provoked by exertion/stress and relieved by rest or antianginal therapy. New, accelerating, prolonged or rest symptoms require ACS evaluation; stable disease is managed with secondary prevention, symptom control and selective testing/revascularization assessment.
recognize: Pressure/heaviness, exertional dyspnea or reduced exercise tolerance can be ischemic equivalents.
A normal resting ECG does not exclude chronic coronary disease.
differentiate: Rest or crescendo symptoms are not stable angina.
Musculoskeletal/reflux syndromes may coexist, but exertional pattern and cardiovascular risk remain important.
assessment: Characterize trigger, duration, relief, functional limitation, risk factors and current antiplatelet/lipid/BP/antianginal therapy.
workup: Select exercise ECG, stress imaging or CCTA according to baseline ECG, exercise capacity and pretest probability when testing will change care.
Do not route suspected ACS through routine outpatient stress testing.
management: Use antiplatelet therapy when indicated, intensive lipid/risk-factor management and antianginal medications individualized to BP/HR/comorbidity.
Refer for cardiology/revascularization assessment for refractory symptoms or high-risk features.
medicationSafety: Nitrates can cause hypotension and are contraindicated with recent PDE-5 inhibitor exposure.
Beta-blockers/non-DHP calcium-channel blockers can cause bradycardia/AV block when combined in susceptible patients.
counselling: Teach when to stop activity, use prescribed rescue therapy and call emergency services rather than repeatedly treating worsening rest symptoms at home.
followUp: Track symptom frequency, activity tolerance and secondary-prevention adherence.
examTrap: Calling a changed/rest pain pattern stable because the patient has a prior diagnosis of angina.
oneLinePearl: Stable angina has a stable pattern; pattern change is an ACS question.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society coronary disease/secondary prevention resources

title: Acute Coronary Syndrome: ECG, Serial Troponin, and Time-Critical Disposition
bottomLine: Suspected ACS is a time-sensitive serial diagnosis based on symptoms, ECG and high-sensitivity troponin in context. Obtain an ECG promptly, activate emergency/reperfusion pathways when indicated, and do not discharge a concerning early presentation because the first ECG or troponin is normal.
recognize: Pressure/heaviness, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, fatigue or epigastric discomfort may be ischemic.
Women, older adults and people with diabetes may present without classic central chest pain.
differentiate: Aortic dissection, PE, tension pneumothorax, esophageal rupture and pericarditis are dangerous alternatives.
Troponin elevation indicates myocardial injury but MI requires ischemic context.
assessment: Assess ABCs, hemodynamics, onset/trajectory, bleeding risk, medication/substance exposure, aortic/PE features and prior CAD.
workup: Obtain urgent 12-lead ECG and repeat if symptoms/electrical findings evolve; use serial high-sensitivity troponin according to the local validated pathway.
Use additional imaging/labs to evaluate competing diagnoses without delaying reperfusion when STEMI is clear.
management: Activate EMS/acute-care pathway, provide guideline-directed antiplatelet/anticoagulant/anti-ischemic therapy after contraindication review, and arrange rapid reperfusion for STEMI through the regional system.
NSTEMI/unstable presentations require risk-based cardiology/invasive strategy.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine oxygen in a normoxemic patient; use oxygen for hypoxemia/respiratory distress.
Nitrates can be unsafe with hypotension, RV infarction/preload dependence or recent PDE-5 inhibitors; antithrombotics require bleeding/aortic-dissection review.
counselling: Explain why transient symptom improvement or one early negative test does not make discharge safe when the presentation remains high risk.
followUp: After ACS, ensure secondary prevention, cardiac rehabilitation, medication reconciliation and closed-loop cardiology follow-up.
examTrap: Ruling out ACS from one normal early troponin or sending STEMI for outpatient testing.
oneLinePearl: ACS is serial: symptoms plus ECG plus time-appropriate troponin.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society ACS/secondary prevention resources

title: Valvular Heart Disease: Let Symptoms and Structure Decide the Urgency
bottomLine: A murmur is a clue, not a diagnosis. Determine timing/location/radiation and symptoms, then use echocardiography when structural disease is plausible. Exertional syncope, angina, heart failure, cyanosis or a new murmur in infection/after MI warrants urgent structural/cardiology assessment.
recognize: Aortic stenosis can cause exertional dyspnea, angina and syncope; regurgitant lesions can cause volume-overload heart failure and arrhythmia.
New murmur with fever can reflect infective endocarditis; new murmur after MI can signal mechanical complication.
differentiate: Innocent murmurs in an otherwise well person differ from pathologic murmurs with abnormal pulses, cyanosis, symptoms or chamber effects.
MVP/click alone does not determine MR severity or prophylaxis needs.
assessment: Assess timing, location/radiation, intensity, pulses, BP, JVP, heart-failure signs, exertional symptoms, fever/endocarditis risk and pregnancy.
workup: Use echocardiography when structural disease is suspected or symptoms/signs warrant it; ECG/chest imaging/labs answer associated rhythm/HF/infection questions.
management: Refer significant valve disease according to severity, symptoms and ventricular response; manage HF/arrhythmia complications while arranging definitive care.
Urgent evaluation is required for acute severe regurgitation, symptomatic severe stenosis or endocarditis/mechanical-complication concern.
medicationSafety: Avoid aggressive preload reduction in severe fixed outflow obstruction when unstable.
Endocarditis prophylaxis is limited to selected highest-risk conditions/procedures, not every murmur or valve lesion.
counselling: Explain that follow-up depends on the confirmed lesion and severity, not how loud the murmur sounds.
followUp: Track symptom change and echo surveillance at clinically appropriate intervals; close the loop on structural-heart referral.
examTrap: Giving dental antibiotic prophylaxis for every murmur—or reassuring exertional syncope because the murmur has been present for years.
oneLinePearl: Murmur intensity is not the treatment plan; symptoms and structural severity are.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society valvular heart disease resources
